title: Week 4 · Lesson 13: Cardiac Electrophysiology & Arrhythmias — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 4 — Lesson 13: Cardiac Electrophysiology & Arrhythmias

FNP-level goal

Use an organized rhythm framework to connect electrical mechanisms with perfusion, identify atrial fibrillation and dangerous ventricular rhythms, recognize electrolyte and ischemic triggers, and decide when a patient needs emergency care rather than outpatient monitoring.

Learning Objectives

  • Describe normal cardiac conduction and the P wave, QRS complex, and T wave.
  • Use rate, regularity, P waves, PR interval, QRS width, and clinical stability as a first ECG framework.
  • Explain atrial fibrillation, reentry-related SVT, bradyarrhythmia, VT, and VF.
  • Connect AF to thromboembolism and potassium/magnesium abnormalities to electrical risk.
  • Recognize hemodynamic instability and emergency red flags in an arrhythmia presentation.

Part 1 — Normal conduction and ECG foundations

The usual electrical pathway is SA node → atria → AV node → His bundle → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibers → ventricles. The SA node is the normal pacemaker. Atrial depolarization corresponds primarily to the P wave; ventricular depolarization to the QRS complex; and ventricular repolarization to the T wave.

The AV node creates a short delay so atria can contract before ventricles. This organized sequence supports filling and cardiac output. A rhythm is not clinically “normal” merely because an ECG label sounds benign; rate, symptoms, perfusion, and the patient’s underlying disease all matter.

Part 2 — A practical first rhythm approach

When you see an ECG or monitor strip, begin systematically: 1) rate, 2) regularity, 3) P waves, 4) PR interval, 5) QRS width, 6) patient stability. This is more reliable than attempting to memorize isolated patterns without clinical context.

Ask early whether the rhythm is causing hypotension, altered mental status, ischemic chest discomfort, severe dyspnea/pulmonary edema, shock, or syncope. Those features define urgency because they signal inadequate perfusion or an immediately dangerous rhythm.

Part 3 — Rate and cardiac output

Recall: cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. A very slow rate can lower cardiac output directly. A very fast rate shortens diastole, reducing ventricular filling and potentially lowering stroke volume; it also raises myocardial oxygen demand and can worsen ischemia. The meaningful question is not only “is the rate above or below 60?” but is the patient perfusing adequately?

Part 4 — Bradycardia and conduction disease

Bradycardia can be physiologic in a well-conditioned asymptomatic person. It becomes clinically important when associated with dizziness, syncope, hypotension, confusion, chest discomfort, or heart failure symptoms. Causes can include medication effects, ischemia, metabolic/electrolyte disturbance, intrinsic conduction disease, or high-grade AV block.

In first-degree AV block, every atrial impulse conducts but the PR interval is prolonged: delayed, not dropped. In higher-grade block, some or all atrial impulses fail to reach the ventricles, potentially causing marked bradycardia and low output.

Part 5 — Supraventricular tachycardia and reentry

SVT is a broad term for fast rhythms arising above the ventricles. A common presentation is abrupt-onset, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia with palpitations, lightheadedness, dyspnea, or chest discomfort. Many SVTs involve reentry: an impulse repeatedly travels through a circuit and re-excites tissue instead of terminating after refractory tissue blocks it.

Even a narrow-complex tachycardia needs context. A stable young patient and an older patient with CAD, heart failure, hypotension, or ischemic symptoms should not be treated as equivalent risk scenarios.

Part 6 — Atrial fibrillation: electrical, hemodynamic, and thrombotic consequences

In atrial fibrillation (AF), multiple disorganized atrial impulses replace organized atrial contraction. Typical ECG reasoning is no consistent P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm. Loss of atrial contraction can reduce ventricular filling, especially in a stiff ventricle such as HFpEF.

Ineffective atrial contraction promotes blood stasis, particularly in the left atrial appendage. Stasis can lead to thrombus, embolization, and ischemic stroke. AF assessment therefore includes stability, ventricular rate, symptom burden, duration, trigger evaluation, structural heart disease, and individualized thromboembolic/bleeding-risk decision-making. Anticoagulation decisions require current guideline-based assessment; they are not determined by rhythm label alone.

Part 7 — AF triggers and connected systems

Common AF associations include age, hypertension, heart failure, valvular disease, coronary disease, obesity, sleep apnea, alcohol exposure, and hyperthyroidism. New AF is a reason to look for reversible contributors and connected conditions. For example: hypertension → LVH/HFpEF/atrial enlargement → AF risk; hyperthyroidism → increased adrenergic activity → AF risk; mitral stenosis → LA enlargement → AF and embolic risk.

Part 8 — Ventricular rhythms: treat the risk seriously

Premature ventricular contractions originate in the ventricles and often produce a wide, abnormal QRS. Occasional PVCs can occur in healthy people, but frequency, symptoms, structural heart disease, ischemia, stimulant exposure, and electrolyte abnormalities change the risk context.

Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is a rapid ventricular rhythm, commonly wide-complex, that can markedly reduce output through poor filling and inefficient contraction. A prior MI can create scar and abnormal conduction pathways that promote reentry and VT. Wide-complex tachycardia with instability should be treated as a dangerous ventricular rhythm until proven otherwise.

Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is chaotic ventricular electrical activity. The ventricles quiver rather than contract effectively, so cardiac output is essentially absent. Collapse, unresponsiveness, absent normal breathing, or no pulse signals cardiac arrest and needs immediate emergency response, CPR, and defibrillation/AED when available.

Part 9 — Electrolytes and medication review

Cardiac conduction depends on potassium, sodium, calcium, and magnesium gradients. Hyperkalemia and hypokalemia can both destabilize electrical activity; CKD, diuretics, RAAS-blocking drugs, GI loss, DKA, and supplements are important clues. Hyperkalemia can cause peaked T waves, PR prolongation, QRS widening, and severe conduction disturbance, but ECG findings are not sensitive enough to exclude clinically significant hyperkalemia.

Prolonged QT represents delayed ventricular repolarization and can predispose to torsades de pointes. Medication review is essential because many drugs, together with hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, bradycardia, or congenital predisposition, can increase QT-related risk.

Part 10 — Syncope: do not stop at “fainting”

A transient arrhythmia can abruptly reduce cardiac output and cerebral perfusion, causing syncope; the ECG can be normal by the time the patient is assessed. History matters: exertional or supine syncope, palpitations before loss of consciousness, known structural heart disease, family history of sudden death, chest pain, or abnormal vital signs require heightened concern and appropriate urgent evaluation.

Case 1 — Irregular palpitations

A 76-year-old has fatigue, palpitations, pulse 122 and irregular, and an ECG with no consistent P waves and irregularly spaced QRS complexes. AF is likely. Next questions are not optional: Is the patient stable? Is there heart failure or ischemia? How fast is the ventricular response? What is the stroke risk? Is a trigger such as thyroid disease, infection, alcohol, or electrolyte disturbance present?

Case 2 — Sudden regular tachycardia

A 35-year-old has abrupt palpitations at 190/min, regular rhythm, narrow QRS, and no instability. SVT with reentry is plausible. However, if chest pain, hypotension, severe dyspnea, syncope, or altered mentation develops, disposition changes immediately to emergency evaluation.

Case 3 — CKD and a dangerous ECG

A patient with CKD has weakness, potassium 7.0 mEq/L, and ECG abnormalities. The mechanism is reduced renal potassium excretion → altered membrane electrophysiology → conduction/arrhythmia risk. This is an urgent emergency problem, not a routine laboratory call-back.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Assess stability before naming the rhythm.
  2. Apply rate, regularity, P waves, PR, and QRS width systematically.
  3. Link the rhythm to perfusion: cardiac output, blood pressure, symptoms, and oxygenation.
  4. Search for triggers: ischemia, HF, thyroid disease, infection, medications, and electrolytes.
  5. For AF, think rate, symptoms, structure, triggers, and stroke-risk assessment.
  6. For wide-complex tachycardia, severe hyperkalemia, VF, or unstable symptoms, arrange emergency care.

High-Yield Summary

Normal pathway: SA → AV → His → bundle branches → Purkinje.
ECG: P = atrial depolarization; QRS = ventricular depolarization; T = ventricular repolarization.
AF: disorganized atrial activity → irregularly irregular rhythm → stasis/thromboembolic risk.
SVT: often rapid, regular, narrow-complex; reentry is common.
VT/VF: ventricular electrical instability can cause shock or arrest.
Electrolytes: potassium and magnesium abnormalities can trigger dangerous rhythms.
Emergency red flags: hypotension, altered mentation, ischemic pain, severe dyspnea/pulmonary edema, shock, syncope, collapse, or no pulse.
